camps.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
camps.why: Flat, sheltered sites in trees with a spring beside them; this route and the Pernod and Whine faces are reached from the bench, so a two-night base is easy.

camps.name: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
camps.why: Saves vertical on summit morning but is windy, cramped and short of water late season; choose it only to link spires from the col.

camps.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
camps.why: A roadside campground for the night before an early start. It is not on the approach, and it closes when the highway shuts for winter.

camps.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side
camps.why: A fallback bivy for a party caught by dark or thirst on the talus. Water is patchy up there, so it is not a planned stop.

plan_conflict: The Burgundy Col camp was main on file, but this plan and the bench's base-camp use put both nights at the bench; the col is demoted to route.

camps.name: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
camps.why: Puts the Rebel Yell base under an hour away, with snow for water; the sites are few, small and windy, and water can vanish late season.

camps.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
camps.why: The calmer, treed camp with a spring. Pick it when the col is windy or full; the summit approach then starts about 1,300 ft lower.

plan_conflict: The bench camp was also main on file; with one night in the plan and parties sleeping at the col for this spire, the bench is demoted to route.

new_camps.name: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
new_camps.why: Closest sleep to Chianti's east face, under an hour away, with snow for water; sites are few and exposed, so it suits a small party in settled weather.
new_camps.water: Snow patches near the col; hard to find late in a dry summer.
new_camps.capacity: Three or four bivy sites, only one big enough for a two-person tent.
new_camps.permit: None needed; the spire lies outside the national park.
new_camps.notes: Elevation is quoted from about 7,720 to 7,950 ft depending on the source. Windy and exposed.

new_camps.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
new_camps.why: Calmer, treed camp with a spring below the col; choose it for shelter at the cost of about 1,300 more ft to climb to the col next morning.
new_camps.water: A spring on the climbers-left side of the bench; thin by late summer.
new_camps.permit: None needed; outside the national park.
new_camps.notes: Quoted between 6,400 and 6,500 ft. Heavy mosquitoes early in the season.

plan_conflict: The plan allows either the bench or the col on night 1; research on the neighbouring Rebel Yell puts most parties at the col, so the col is main.

camps.why: The west face is reached by a gully straight from the bench, so there is no need to climb to the col; flat sites in trees with a nearby spring.

camps.name: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
camps.why: A higher, windier camp used by parties linking several spires; it adds a climb to the col and a long drop back to the face.

camps.name: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
camps.why: The standard line starts across the col and under the east walls, so sleeping here shortens the climb; sites are small and windy with snow for water.

camps.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
camps.why: Sheltered, with a spring and room to spread out; it adds roughly 1,300 ft of climbing to the col on summit morning.

camps.name: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
camps.why: Same trip as the standard line: sleep at the col to start from the notch side next morning; sites are small and windy with snow for water.

camps.name: Meadows below the Silver Horn's south face
camps.why: The only camp near the route: meadows right under the south face, so summit day starts at the base and you rappel back to your tent.

camps.name: Meadows below the Silver Horn's south face
camps.why: The only camp near the route: meadows right under the south face, so summit day starts at the base and you rappel back to your tent.

camps.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
camps.why: The sheltered, treed camp most parties pick for the glacier, with a spring; it makes summit day longer than sleeping at the col.

camps.name: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
camps.why: Puts you at the glacier's doorstep for a shorter summit day, but the few sites are cramped and windy and water depends on snow.

camps.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
camps.why: A roadside campground for the night before an early start. It is not on the approach, and it closes when the highway shuts for winter.

camps.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side
camps.why: A fallback bivy for a party caught by dark or thirst on the talus. Water is patchy up there, so it is not a planned stop.

plan_conflict: Bench and col were both main on file; with one night only, the plan's most-parties choice, the bench, stays main and the col becomes route. Some parties do sleep at the col.

camps.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
camps.why: The established camp on this side, with a nearby spring and the shortest hike from the highway; the ridge traverse starts by gaining the col next morning.

camps.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
camps.why: A full-day climb with a slow descent gully is best done from a settled base: flat treed sites, a spring nearby, and no carry to the col.

camps.name: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
camps.why: Higher and windier with little water late season; only worth it to string other spires together, since Whine's route is approached from below.

camps.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
camps.why: A roadside campground for the night before an early start. It is not on the approach, and it closes when the highway shuts for winter.

camps.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side
camps.why: A fallback bivy for a party caught by dark or thirst on the talus. Water is patchy up there, so it is not a planned stop.

plan_conflict: The col and Lone Fir were main on file; the plan and the camp-to-camp climbing times point to the bench for both nights, so the others become route.

camps.name: Snowy Lakes basin
camps.why: The standard camp for Tower and Golden Horn: lakeside sites with water, close enough that summit day is a light pack and a return to tents.

camps.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
camps.why: The start of the walk, not a place anyone sleeps on the trip; a toilet but no water, and the camps start miles up the trail.

camps.name: Cutthroat Pass, PCT crest camps
camps.why: A first stopping point about five miles in with several sites, but it is exposed and a long way from the climb; a late party might stop here.

camps.name: Granite Pass
camps.why: A few sites halfway to the lakes that break the walk in two; useful for a late start but it leaves a longer first morning toward the peak.

plan_conflict: Rainy Pass trailhead was main on file but nobody sleeps there on this trip; Snowy Lakes basin is the one main for night 1.

camps.name: Gargett Mine basin bivy
camps.why: A small basin close under the peak's approach ridge; it turns the long off-trail day into two, but sites are few and water thins out late in the season.

camps.name: High Pass camp
camps.why: A marginal, exposed spot near the start of the cross-country; a party that runs short of daylight or finds the basin full may stop here.

camps.name: Twin Lakes basin road-end camp
camps.why: A drive-up campground with toilets for a rested start; it adds the whole approach to the summit day and has no drinking water.

camps.name: Upper Diobsud Lakes
camps.why: The plan's traverse ends here: lake water and flat benches, and the summit is a round trip from camp the next day.

camps.name: Northeast Bacon camp, above the glacier
camps.why: A higher camp half a mile from the summit that suits a two-day push or carrying over after the climb; it is waterless late in the season.

camps.name: Watson Lakes designated camps
camps.why: A short two-mile walk from the road with lake water; stop here if starting late, then do the long traverse the following day.

camps.name: Lower Anderson Lake
camps.why: Sits directly below the climbers' ridge route, so it works for a late start; the plan walks past it on day one.

camps.name: Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
camps.why: The trailhead on a gravel road; sleep here only for an early start the next morning, not as a camp on the trip.

plan_conflict: Research for the standard two-day trip names a high camp near the summit rather than Diobsud Lakes; the plan's three-day shape with Diobsud both nights could not be confirmed.

new_camps.name: Upper Blum Lake
new_camps.why: The natural base for the glacier side: lake water and good sites at the end of the steep path, with the summit a round trip from camp.
new_camps.permit: Backcountry permit needed; the area is inside the national park, with parties limited to six.
new_camps.notes: The Blum Lakes are reached by the faint climbers' path from Blum Creek; the lakes sit near 4,900 to 5,000 ft.

camps.name: South Hagan bench
camps.why: Open benches on Hagan's south side where parties stage for the south slopes; it is the closest sleep to the climb, with long carries to reach it.

camps.name: Hidden Lake, below the Blum-Hagan divide
camps.why: Reliable water on the far side of Hagan, used by parties traversing east; it sits well below the bench and adds a climb to the south slopes.

camps.name: Sulphide Camp, end of the Baker River trail
camps.why: Built sites and a toilet at trail's end, but off the climbers' route; it suits a trail-only trip, not Hagan, and adds a long bushwhack.

plan_conflict: The plan camps on benches above Diobsud Lakes, which is not a camp on file; South Hagan bench is the nearest listed camp but the match was not confirmed.

camps.name: Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
camps.why: Snow camp just past the first notch from Ruth, about 6,600 ft; it puts Icy a few hours away on day two and leaves a drop and haul out afterward.

camps.name: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
camps.why: Drier rock sites at the toe of the glacier; use them to split the walk-in or for Ruth alone, but they leave a longer day to Icy.

camps.name: Ruth Mountain summit camp
camps.why: A view-rich snow camp on Ruth's dome that is a popular choice, though it is windy and a longer way from Icy than the notch.

camps.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
camps.why: A road-end camp for a late arrival before the alpine start; it adds the whole walk-in to the next day.

plan_conflict: Ruth Arm ridge camps and Ruth summit camp were both main on file; the plan and research put night 1 at the notch beyond Ruth, so those two become route.
